doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Hits Dorn could not hear: Where Is the Love and Killing Me Softly
summary: Dorn lost his hit-picking ears at Atlantic. He tells of Where Is the Love, and of Killing Me Softly, when he threatened to quit over Ahmet's objections to the drum sound.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: It’s hard to recognize a hit, isn’t it?

Sometimes. I could pick a hit track off of any kind of album when I was a disc jockey. Within six months of coming to Atlantic I lost my disc jockey ears. You have no idea. Listen I had a hit with Roberta Flack and Donny Hathaway that Arif Martin and I co- produced. It was called “Where is the Love.”

Until the last day before they went to the pressing plant I was trying to take it off the album. And the thing that stopped me was I was walking through the hall and one of the secretaries, Barbara Harris, she said, “I heard the test pressing on Roberta and Donny.” I said, “yeah.” She said, “wow you’ve got a smash.” I said, “what is it?” She said, “what do you mean what is it?” I said, “what is it?” She said, “Where is the Love.” You know, like what are you an idiot. I said, “really?” She said, “yeah.” I said, “oh okay.” I figured if the secretaries liked it, they knew more about what was good or bad than I did. I just didn’t always have those kind of ears. I knew “Killing Me Softly” was a hit. I knew that was a hit. In fact I knew it was going to win the Grammy. So, one of the few times I knew I had a hit Atlantic didn’t like it. They wanted me to remix it. They didn’t like the

drum, that big fat, you know footed bass boom. And I said, “well that’s the record.” I actually had to threaten to quit. I went to Nesuhi because Ahmet hated it. And I went to Nesuhi and I said, “look I can’t do this anymore.” I said, “that’s a smash, that’s a number one record, that’s a Grammy winner.” So he went to bat for me. Ahmet and I were never right after that.
The beginning of it sounds like it was done in a big church.

You want to hear what the beginning was? We wanted to have her do like some vocalese in the beginning, this kind of word thing. So she did seven or eight takes. And if you notice, they’re mono. We put them all off in the corner someplace, made a little mix of those voices. And then at the end we put them in. And it was, wow. And people said like “how did you get that?” The cavernous — you know and how we got it was it all ended up on one track, there was nothing you could do with it and it sounded good so we put it on. Let me tell you something. Are you starting to see a picture here?
